name: Dull Purple
lede: Dull Purple is a muted reddish purple; the name is a plain modifier, and the books use the phrase for puce and for what happens when painters mix red, yellow and blue.

sections.title: One swatch, many standards
sections.body: The swatch appears in the ISCC-NBS list of 1955, the RAL chart of 1927 and the xkcd survey of 2010, and the nearest ISCC-NBS name is "moderate reddish purple", 3.8 units away [1]. It is a darker, redder cousin of [[mauve]] and sits near [[eggplant]].

sections.title: Puce, a dull purple
sections.body: Paterson lists four senses for puce: dull purple, brownish purple, pinkish blue and dark red [2]. The word comes from the Latin *pulex*, flea, whose underside is puce in color [2]. The disagreement shows how loose dull purples are as names, which is why [[puce]] is hard to pin to one swatch.

sections.title: The mixing problem
sections.body: Westland points to Moses Harris's hue circle of 1776, in his book on English insects, and says a spot color in one segment suggests Harris knew that mixing red, yellow and blue primaries produced dull purples [3].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: Only 4 of 23,781 archive paintings contain it, rarer than 79 per cent of named colors, and the earliest dated one is by Paul Gauguin, from 1903 [4]. These are photographs of varnished paintings, so the count says little about how often painters used muted purples [4].
